subject: SecureBank: transport anchoring — peering vs PrivateLink vs site-to-site VPN
messages:
From: Sylvia Nguyen <sylvia.nguyen@securebank.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Cc: Raj Patel <raj.patel@securebank.com>
Date: Mon, 24 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SecureBank requirements + ask: recommended connectivity approach

Hi Neha / Kimberly,

Thanks again for the quick sync yesterday. Attached is a short requirements doc that summarizes our networking and security constraints for Redwood Private (SecureBank pilot). High level constraints: no internet egress from our data center (all outbound traffic must be anchored to specific IP blocks), deep packet inspection & source IP preservation for audit, strict mutual TLS or IPsec, and an SLA requirement for 99.95% with predictable latency (sub-60ms to your hosted pods in east-us-2).

We'd like Redwood's recommendation between the three primary patterns you present in the sales playbook: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN / IPsec. In particular, we care about:
- Attack surface / lateral movement risk (are there transitive routing concerns?)
- How source IP visibility is preserved for our IDS and logging
- Operational complexity (maintenance, cert rotation, failover)
- Compliance evidence we can show auditors (where to find network logs, flow logs, audit trail)

Can you send a short comparison and your recommended path for a security-first regulated customer? If you could also include the minimum network and firewall changes required on our side for the recommended option, that would be helpful.

I've attached SecureBank_Requirements.pdf.

Regards,
Sylvia Nguyen
Head of Network Security
SecureBank

Subject: Re: SecureBank requirements + ask: recommended connectivity approach

Sylvia — thanks for the doc and the clear constraints. Quick summary up front: for a high-assurance regulated customer with requirements you outlined, our recommendation is to prefer PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for primary connectivity and keep site-to-site VPN as an operational fallback for full-control or lift-and-shift scenarios. VPC peering is acceptable in narrow circumstances but generally raises transitive routing and surface-area concerns we try to avoid for regulated tenants.

Below is a concise pros/cons table and the minimum changes we expect on SecureBank's firewall side. Connor and Karthik added technical footnotes below.

Recommended (primary): PrivateLink (interface endpoint)
- Pros: endpoint-level access, no cross-account route propagation, easier to enforce granular policy, preserves destination affinity (your traffic terminates at a private endpoint we control), minimal attack surface, best fit when customers require endpoint-level allow lists.
- Cons: requires endpoint provisioning and ENI/routing in your VPC, potential cost for per-endpoint data processing; requires TLS/mTLS configuration for mutual auth.

Fallback / secondary: Site-to-site VPN (IPsec)
- Pros: straightforward for existing on-prem gear, predictable IPsec lifecycle, useful when you need complete L3 access to the VPC for multiple services.
- Cons: NAT may obscure original source IP unless you arrange for 1:1 mappings; typically larger blast radius and harder to lock down to per-service policies.

VPC Peering (not recommended as primary)
- Pros: low-latency direct routing, simple routing once established.
- Cons: routing can be transitive within your VPCs if not carefully managed; cross-account peering requires explicit route management and still exposes broader subnet-level reachability (worse from compliance perspective).

Minimum firewall changes (PrivateLink recommended):
- Allow outbound TCP 443 to our interface endpoint ENI IP range (we will provide the exact IPs).
- Open port 443 inbound from your NAT / edge devices to the endpoint's private IPs if you are using internal routing.
- Allow BGP only for managed failover, otherwise avoid advertising broad prefixes into Redwood VPCs.

Next steps:
1) Connor: can you add a short tech note (attached) with IP preservation details and a suggested canary test?
2) We will produce a draft MOP + pilot test plan and share.
3) If SecureBank wants full L3 access after pilot, we'll run a short security review to scope peering with strict ACLs.

-Neha

Thanks Sylvia — a few concrete technical notes from our infra team (short):

1) Source IP preservation
- PrivateLink: preserves client source IPs only when traffic does not traverse NAT inside the customer's network. If your edge NAT rewrites source IPs, you'll need to either preserve mappings (1:1) or collect original-IP headers at application layer. For audit, we recommend enabling VPC Flow Logs both on your VPC subnets and the interface endpoint ENIs; we can provide the endpoint IDs so you can stitch logs together.
- VPN (IPsec): by default many VPN endpoints perform SNAT. To preserve source IPs across an IPsec tunnel you must configure policy-based routing or specific phase-2 selectors; this is vendor-dependent (we've documented common configs for Cisco/Juniper/Palo Alto).
- Peering: preserves source/dest IPs natively, but creates a broader network surface — hard to carve per-service ACLs.

2) Failover and HA
- PrivateLink: create two interface endpoints in separate AZs, and test endpoint health via our health-checks. We can offer a cross-AZ failover plan in the MOP.
- VPN: ensure active/standby tunnels, advertise prefixes with low BFD timers; test failover windows (we typically see 10–20s depending on hardware).

3) IDS / DPI visibility
- For best auditability, enable flow logs and forward to your SIEM. If deep packet inspection is mandatory on plaintext traffic, we recommend terminating TLS at your side where policy permits — otherwise provide us with proof-of-encryption and certificate metadata for audit.

Attachment: quick-tech-notes.txt (short vendor commands and a one-page canary plan).

-Connor

Raj / Sylvia — attached is a draft MOP and a pilot test plan (pilot-test-plan.xlsx). Highlights and commitments:

- Pilot window: Sep 7 — Sep 18 (10 business days). Proposed activities: endpoint provisioning (day 0–2), canary latency & functionality tests (day 3–5), failover drills and cert rotation test (day 6–8), audit collection and evidence handoff (day 9–10).
- Cert rotation: Redwood can provide managed mTLS for the interface endpoint during the pilot to reduce operational friction; for production we support customer-managed certs via your PKI (we'll exchange CSR/CA bundles). We'll include the certificate lifetime, rotation cadence, and audit epoch in the MOP.
- Flow logs / audit evidence: we'll provide VPC Flow Logs for the interface endpoint ENIs and a consolidated audit bundle (gz) with time-series for the pilot window. You can ingest into your SIEM or we can push to a preconfigured S3 bucket (SecureBank-owned).
- Acceptance criteria: consistent sub-60ms median token roundtrip, zero unauthorized connection attempts during pilot, successful cert rotation without connectivity loss.

Attachments: redwood-mop-draft.docx, pilot-test-plan.xlsx

Action items:
- Sylvia: confirm the pilot window and whether SecureBank prefers Redwood-managed certs during pilot.
- SecureBank network team: provide contact for endpoint provisioning (ticket with IP allowlist).
- Karthik: please create a short runbook snippet for peering-safe fallback in case SecureBank later requests L3 access.

We'll set up a 30-min kickoff after Sylvia confirms.
